findings.claim: [the textbook names] bounded rationality that collapses a complex incident to one obvious cause
findings.failure_mode: applied consequence presented as what the source names
findings.evidence: Deep 185: bounded rationality = cognitive limits prevent fully rational treatment of complex issues. Source 8286-8300: we cannot fully grasp all alternatives or implications, and information is often incomplete. Neither says it collapses events to a single cause; that is the distillation's extrapolation.
findings.fix: correct: bounded rationality, the limit on how much of a complex situation anyone can grasp, which leaves room for a complex incident to be reduced to one obvious cause

findings.claim: ... and when the encoding-decoding-noise communication model explains why two participants experienced the same event differently.
findings.evidence: Deep 334: the model covers a communicator encoding a message and a receiver decoding it, with noise distorting clarity (source 16348-16352). It is about message transmission, not about witnessing an event. The source's own explanation for 'employees looking at the same event often see substantially different things' is the attribution biases (source 3945-3947, Ch 3.3) and perceptual selectivity (Ch 3.1).
findings.fix: correct: ... and why two participants can see the same event differently: the text says the attribution biases 'help us understand why employees looking at the same event often see substantially different things' (Ch 3.3), and perceptual selectivity explains the rest (Ch 3.1). cycle-to-deep: source 3945-3947.

findings.claim: This is the primary driver of blame language.
findings.failure_mode: overstated; supporting passage absent from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 81 carries only the FAE definition. Source 3939-3940 adds: 'Hence, when a major problem occurs within a certain department, we tend to blame people rather than events or situations.' The source supports FAE driving blame, not that it is the primary driver.
findings.fix: correct: The text draws the consequence itself: 'when a major problem occurs within a certain department, we tend to blame people rather than events or situations.' cycle-to-deep: source 3939-3940 (Ch 3.3, 'Attributional Bias').

findings.claim: Actor-observer bias. Observers attribute others' behaviour dispositionally; actors attribute their own behaviour situationally ... (Source: Ch 3.3, 'Attributional Bias')
findings.failure_mode: concept not in deep or source, attributed to the source
findings.evidence: Deep 77-81 (Ch 3.3) names only the fundamental attribution error and the self-serving bias. Source 3931-3947: 'Two such errors, or attribution biases, should be noted here' (FAE and self-serving bias). grep 'actor-observer' in the converted source: 0 hits. The concept is held by openstax-psychology-2e deep 277 (Ch 12.1).
findings.fix: strip (or re-attribute: Actor-observer bias is held in the corpus by OpenStax Psychology 2e, Ch 12.1, not by this source)

findings.claim: In AARs: the gap between leadership's account of how clear direction was and workers' account of the same direction is often this large.
findings.failure_mode: empirical magnitude claim extrapolated from different data
findings.evidence: Deep 71 and source 3515-3538 (Table 3.1): Likert's data measure how often supervisors give forms of recognition, as seen by each side. Nothing in the deep or source measures gaps in accounts of how clear direction was, or says such gaps are 'often this large'.
findings.fix: correct: In AARs: leadership's and workers' accounts of how clear direction was can diverge in the same way; Likert's data show how wide a vertical perceptual gap can run.

findings.evidence: Deep 189 lists confirmation bias under barrier 5, personal biases. Source 8343 '##### Personal Biases' carries it (8368-8370); the 'Conflict' subsection starts at 8386 and does not mention it.

findings.claim: The Asch conformity finding: "in over a third of trials, subjects denied the evidence of their own senses to agree with a unanimous group" [BT].
findings.failure_mode: deep-ref paraphrase in quotation marks presented as the source's words
findings.evidence: Deep 294 is the deep ref's paraphrase. Source 13882-13884: 'In over one-third of the trials in the experiment, the naive subject denied the evidence of his own senses and agreed with the answers given by the unknown confederates.'
findings.fix: correct: The Asch conformity finding: "In over one-third of the trials in the experiment, the naive subject denied the evidence of his own senses and agreed with the answers given by the unknown confederates" [BT].

findings.claim: The basic model ... names why participants who were physically present at the same event can produce accounts that seem to describe different incidents. Noise is not malice or memory failure; it is the structural condition of organisational communication.
findings.failure_mode: concept applied outside its scope; overstated
findings.evidence: Deep 334 and source 16326-16352: the model concerns a message passing from communicator to receiver; decoding is shaped by the receiver's experience and frame of reference; noise is 'factors that distort message clarity' and 'can occur at any point along the model'. Nothing about eyewitness accounts of an event, and nothing calls noise 'the structural condition of organisational communication'.
findings.fix: correct: The basic model (communicator encodes, receiver decodes, noise distorts) explains why the same message can land differently: decoding is shaped by each receiver's experience and frame of reference, and noise can enter at any point (Ch 11.1). In AARs it explains divergent readings of the same instruction or alert.

findings.claim: Managers in disturbance/crisis-handler mode are under reactive-system pressure. Decisions made under crisis conditions are less reflective, more heuristic-driven, more confirmation-biased. (Source: Ch 11.3, 'Decisional'; Ch 6.2)
findings.failure_mode: composite synthesis with one unsupported predicate; supporting chapter missing
findings.evidence: Source 16622-16623 (Ch 11.3) says only that crisis handlers 'must involuntarily react to conditions'. Deep 173 and source 8144 (Ch 6.2): intense emotions pull toward the reactive route; deep 187 (Ch 6.4): time pressure pushes toward heuristics. Nothing says crisis conditions raise confirmation bias; source 8373-8375 runs the other way (challenged beliefs push the brain toward the reactive system).
findings.fix: correct: Mintzberg's disturbance or crisis handler must 'involuntarily react to conditions' (Ch 11.3). Crises tend to bring the intense emotion that pulls decisions toward the reactive route (Ch 6.2) and the time pressure that pushes decision-makers onto heuristics (Ch 6.4). (Source: Ch 11.3; Ch 6.2; Ch 6.4)

findings.claim: Need: Actor-observer bias arriving ("they should have known")
findings.failure_mode: question keyed to a concept the source does not hold
findings.evidence: See D004: actor-observer bias is absent from the deep and the converted source.
findings.fix: correct: Need: Fundamental attribution error arriving ("they should have known")

findings.claim: Two participants describe the same event as if they were in different rooms | Encoding-decoding-noise — not inconsistency or dishonesty, but structural perceptual divergence
findings.evidence: As D002/D008: the communication model covers message transmission (deep 334). Divergent accounts of one event map to Ch 3.3 (source 3945-3947) and Ch 3.1 perceptual selectivity (deep 69-71).
findings.fix: correct: Diagnosis: perceptual selectivity and attribution bias (Ch 3.1, Ch 3.3), not inconsistency or dishonesty; where the divergence is over a message or alert, add encoding-decoding-noise (Ch 11.1).

findings.claim: The facilitator applies the Dearborn-Simon perceptual-selectivity frame (Ch 3.1): the operations team's 'clear signal' is the signal as seen from a functional vantage point with full system context; the technician's 'ambiguous dashboard' is the signal as seen from the point of action with incomplete context.
findings.failure_mode: source finding applied to a different mechanism
findings.evidence: Deep 71 and source 3507-3512: Dearborn and Simon gave executives the same case; each saw the problem of their own function as primary. The example's divergence is driven by different information (full vs incomplete context), which is not what the study shows.
findings.fix: correct: the operations team and the technician read the same alert through different roles; as in Dearborn and Simon's study, each sees what their function primes them to see (Ch 3.1). The difference in context each had is a further condition to surface.

findings.claim: the facilitator introduces the bounded-rationality frame (Ch 6.4) ... probing for the five conditions that made non-escalation the locally rational choice: time pressure, authority ambiguity, information state, prior norm, and status asymmetry.
findings.failure_mode: invented enumeration placed under a source citation
findings.evidence: Deep 183-190 (Ch 6.4): bounded rationality is one of six barriers; time constraints and uncertainty are separate barriers; source 8286-8300 ties bounded rationality to cognitive limits and incomplete information. Authority ambiguity, prior norm and status asymmetry are not in the Ch 6.4 frame, and the source gives no five-condition list.
findings.fix: correct: ... probing for the conditions that bounded the technician's choice: incomplete information and time pressure (Ch 6.4), plus the local ones the scenario supplies (authority ambiguity, prior norm, status asymmetry).

findings.claim: SSDL explains why single-cause accounts persist (linear thinking applied to feedback systems); OB explains the cognitive mechanisms — bounded rationality, confirmation bias — that make single-cause accounts feel satisfying
findings.evidence: SSDL deep 17 and 111: feedback structure explains why problems persist; linear 'X causes Y' reasoning can fail. It does not explain why single-cause accounts persist. OB deep 185, 189 define bounded rationality and confirmation bias; neither is said to make single-cause accounts feel satisfying.
findings.fix: correct: SSDL shows where single-cause accounts fail (linear 'X causes Y' reasoning applied to feedback structure); OB names the cognitive limits (bounded rationality, confirmation bias) that make a single cause easy to settle on

findings.claim: The Likert supervisor-subordinate gap data is `[V]` in the deep ref; preserved in Concept 5. (and line 122: Likert's data ... is cited in the source as [BT])
findings.failure_mode: integrity note misstates the file's marker
findings.evidence: Deep 71 marks the Likert data [V]. Concept 5 (line 20) carries it as [BT], so the marker was changed, not preserved; line 122 then calls it [BT] 'in the source'. [BT] fits the relayed data; the quoted row label is the table's wording (source 3530-3531).
findings.fix: correct: The Likert data are [V] in the deep ref (the quoted row label is Table 3.1's wording); Concept 5 carries them as [BT] because the source relays Likert's study.

findings.claim: The source's scaffolding sections ... were excluded from the deep reference coverage scope; all substantive exposition is covered.
findings.evidence: Deep 396: Ch 12.7-12.8 (substitutes for leadership, transformational leadership) are 'sections present but not fully covered in the read'.
findings.fix: correct: ... were excluded from the deep reference coverage scope; the deep ref flags Ch 12.7-12.8 as not fully covered, and all other substantive exposition is covered.

Quote check against the converted source: FAE definition (3937-3939) and 'can actually lead to improved performance' (8416-8417) are word for word; the Likert 80/14 figures and 'sincere and thorough praise' row label match Table 3.1 (3530-3531). The Asch 'quote' is not the source's wording (D007). The derived-from-deep sha256 (a475cbbb...) matches the current deep ref. Integration rows checked against other deep refs: openstax-psychology-2e (hindsight bias 146, Loftus 186, Asch 291, Milgram 291, FAE 275), tc-25-20-army-aar (four-step process 52, open-ended questions 134), lfuo-learning-review-guide-2024 (administrative firewall 67; 'how decisions made sense at the time' 178, 184; the deep does not use the phrase 'local rationality' but carries the concept) hold; the SSDL row drifts (D014). The 'TC 25-20, LFUO and NHS carry those' line holds (nhs-just-culture-guide deep exists and carries just culture). Applied guidance judged faithful: the 'why did they do that?' FAE heuristic, the Phase 5 escalation-of-commitment question (reverting = staying the old course), the cohesiveness-suppresses-dissent claim (deep 298 'group power over members'; source 14137-14141 and 8908-8909, groupthink from team spirit), and the 'relationship conflict almost never does' gloss of 'generally harmful'. Recurring claims listed at each occurrence: actor-observer bias (D004, D010); encoding-decoding as event-perception model (D002, D008, D011). Non-graded observations: the Worked Example carries no verbatim blockquote although the protocol asks for one where the source's words carry a claim; the distillation's only [V] passages are inline in Key Concepts. Deep-ref gaps surfaced (cycling candidates): source 3939-3940 (FAE produces blame of people over situations) and 3945-3947 (the two attribution biases explain why employees see the same event differently) belong in deep Part III; the source's crisis-handler sentence (16622-16623) is not in deep 338-342.
